common_name: Forever Pink Hydrangea (Heat-Tolerant Reblooming Bigleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Forever Pink is an older heat-tolerant bigleaf hydrangea cultivar selected for continuous flowering through summer in warm climates where many mopheads stall out after their first flush.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from the hottest afternoon sun in warm climates. Forever Pink was selected decades ago for its ability to keep producing rounded mophead flower clusters through the heat of summer rather than flowering once and stopping, making it a long-standing favorite in mild-winter, hot-summer regions. Flower color runs pink to rose in neutral to alkaline soil and can shift toward purple-blue tones if the soil is acidified, the same pH-driven color response typical of bigleaf hydrangeas. Keep soil evenly moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly right after flowering to avoid removing the old-wood buds that produce the earliest blooms.

common_name: Let's Dance Starlight Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Let's Dance Starlight is a compact addition to the Let's Dance reblooming series, bred to flower reliably on both old and new wood on a tidy, rounded plant.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade in hot climates. Let's Dance Starlight is part of Bailey Nurseries' Let's Dance series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas, producing large mophead flower clusters on both old wood carried over from the previous season and new growth produced the same year, so a late spring freeze that damages old buds does not eliminate flowering for the year. Its compact, rounded habit fits foundation plantings and large containers better than older full-size mopheads. Flower color shifts from blue-purple in acidic soil to pink in neutral to alkaline soil, adjustable with soil amendments. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch to keep roots cool, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood so as not to sacrifice old-wood flower buds.

common_name: Seaside Serenade Hamptons Hydrangea (Compact Reblooming Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Hamptons is a member of the Seaside Serenade series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas bred for compact size and dense, full mophead flower clusters.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade in warm climates. Hamptons flowers on both old and new wood, giving it a long bloom season from late spring into fall even after a hard winter damages old-wood buds. Its compact, dense habit and full, rounded flower clusters make it well suited to foundation plantings and large containers. Flower color shifts with soil pH, from blue-purple in acidic soil to pink in neutral to alkaline soil. Keep soil evenly moist through summer heat, mulch to protect the root zone, and prune only lightly right after the main flush to avoid removing old-wood buds.

common_name: Tuff Stuff Red Hydrangea (Reblooming Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Tuff Stuff Red is a deeper-flowered member of the Tuff Stuff mountain hydrangea series, flowering on both old and new wood for a long, reliable rebloom window.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun. Tuff Stuff Red is a compact reblooming mountain hydrangea (Hydrangea serrata) that flowers on both old and new growth, so a hard late freeze that damages the previous year's buds does not prevent a strong flush of lacecap blooms later in the season. Its deeper rose-red to pink flower tones stand out among the typically blue or white-flowered members of the Tuff Stuff series, and color still shifts somewhat with soil pH the same way it does in bigleaf hydrangea. Mountain hydrangea is generally more cold-hardy and sun-tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea. Water regularly during dry spells and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat.

common_name: Fire Light Rocket Hydrangea (Narrow Columnar Panicle Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Light Rocket is a narrow, upright-columnar sport of Fire Light, bred for tight spaces where a full-spreading panicle hydrangea would not fit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Light Rocket keeps the sturdy stems and reliable color change of its parent Fire Light but grows in a narrow, upright column rather than spreading wide, making it useful for tight side yards, narrow foundation beds, and vertical accents where standard panicle hydrangeas are too broad. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms on new wood, so it can be pruned hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and its dense white flower clusters age to deep red-pink in late summer and fall. It tolerates more sun and less consistent moisture than mophead hydrangeas once established.
